Honoré-Gabriel Riqueti, Comte de Mirabeau. Born in 1749, this man was the French Revolution's most brilliant and charismatic orator in its early phase. Despite his noble origins, he championed popular sovereignty and constitutional limits on royal power. He was elected as a deputy to the Estates-General in 1789 despite being a noble, and he emerged as the Third Estate's most persuasive voice for reform and popular rights. When Baron de Breteuil demanded that the nobles leave the assembly, Mirabeau delivered a famous riposte: Go tell those who sent you that we are here by the will of the people and shall not leave except by the force of bayonets. He played a central role in the Tennis Court Oath on June 20, 1789, when the National Assembly made its defiant vow to write a constitution. Yet Mirabeau negotiated secretly with the royal court, hoping to preserve the monarchy through a constitutional settlement that would satisfy both reform-minded nobles and popular demands. He chaired the National Assembly and used his oratory to guide early revolutionary legislation, maintaining a vision of moderate, law-based change. He died under mysterious circumstances on April 2, 1791, possibly from a chronic illness worsened by debauchery. After his death, his private papers revealed his royalist dealings. His death removed a potential moderate voice from the assembly just as the revolution was shifting toward radicalism.
